title: Anthony Albanese to slash annual refugee intake
text:
By KYLIE STEVENS, SENIOR BREAKING NEWS REPORTER, AUSTRALIA and AUSTRALIAN ASSOCIATED PRESS

Published:  09:14 AEST, 27 August 2026   |  Updated:  09:21 AEST, 27 August 2026

204

View  comments

The Albanese government will cut Australia's annual refugee intake by a third as part of its crackdown to reduce net overseas migration.

The current annual humanitarian quota, which has risen to 20,000 in recent years, will be slashed to 13,750 in 2027-28.

The cuts are not part of the immigration curbs currently being considered by the Labor cabinet, which is still in tense negotiations over its long-awaited immigration overhaul.

But it has already been factored into budget projections for net overseas migration to drop to 225,000 in 2027-28.

Cuts to refugee levels were also motivated by the strain on resettlement services, a government source told the Australian Financial Review.

Since being elected to power in 2022, Labor has increased the humanitarian intake to 20,000 refugees a year.

The figure is well short of a plan announced by then-Opposition leader Bill Shorten in 2015 to accept 27,000 refugees a year by 2025.

The last annual increase, from 17,875 to 20,000, was in 2023.

The Albanese government will cut Australia's annual refugee intake by a third as part of its crackdown to reduce net overseas migration.

Anthony Albanese has also vowed not to force British backpackers to work in regional Australia as part of the government's looming migration overhaul

'With more people displaced worldwide than ever before, the Albanese Labor government is stepping up to play its part in the global resettlement effort in a responsible way,' then-immigration minister Andrew Giles said at the time.

The Albanese government announced earlier this year that it would slash overseas migration levels, above 300,000, to 245,000 this year and 225,000 next year and in subsequent years.

But its migration policy has been hit by fresh delays; polling confirms the issue is behind a surge of support for One Nation.

Labor was expected to unveil changes to its migration settings in a speech by Burke at the National Press Club earlier this month.

But the address was cancelled at the eleventh hour due to cabinet not agreeing to the changes amid internal division.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese warned it would be some time before the policy is finalised.

'We have a series of plans in place. There's more work to do, and we'll work on that and make announcements at appropriate times,' he told ABC Radio on Tuesday.

'We want to make sure we get it right, and we have got migration policy as front and centre.'

Labor has been under pressure in the polls amid growing support for Pauline Hanson

Albanese has also vowed not to force British backpackers to work in regional Australia as part of the government's looming migration overhaul.

There had been speculation Labor could reverse a rule introduced under Australia's free trade agreement with the UK.

The change removed the requirement for British backpackers to spend three months working in regional Australia to qualify for a second or third year in the country.

Since the new rules came into effect last year, the number of British backpackers in Australia has surged from about 47,000 to 80,000.

'The UK situation is a separate agreement as a result of the UK free trade agreement which we are certainly honouring,' Albanese said.

Migration numbers have been the focus of debate after One Nation MP David Farley claimed the party's figures would include an extra 100,000 people annually, on top of the 130,000 it had already committed to, making it higher than Labor's.

The comments prompted an intervention from Senator Hanson on social media, stating the party remained committed to a 130,000-person a year target.

Albanese said the incident demonstrated the party was not coherent when it came to migration policy.

'One Nation on Sunday pointed out the hypocrisy when they said 130,000 plus an additional more than 100,000 because you need essential workers in aged care, in agriculture, in all of these areas as well,' he said.

'One of the things that the business community have said to me here in Perth is the importance of skilled migration in construction.'

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor said the Coalition's target would likely be under 200,000 people annually.

'It's got to be a number that we can deal with. What I can say is it'll be substantially below the numbers we have seen in recent years,' he told Seven's Sunrise this week.

'The real mistake we've seen in recent years is to allow the immigration numbers to get way above what we can cope with as a country, and the single most important indicator of that is how many houses we've got.'
